title: The Klondike Gold Rush: How Ordinary Men Survived the Frozen Trail
title_alt: Surviving Chilkoot Pass: The Brutal Reality of the 1897 Yukon Gold Rush
description:
In July eighteen ninety-seven, news of a ton of Alaskan gold reached Seattle and sparked the wild Klondike Gold Rush. Over one hundred thousand men packed up their lives and rushed into the frozen Yukon wilderness, facing impossible mountain passes, starvation, and lethal rapids.

This is the true story of Walt Becker and his partner Sam, two ordinary men who carried a ton of gear up the legendary Golden Stairs of Chilkoot Pass and built a wooden boat to braved the wild North-West territory.

Would you have turned back at the foot of Chilkoot Pass, or would you have kept climbing into the ice? Let us know in the comments below!
pinned_comment: If you were twenty-two years old in 1897, would you have risked everything to haul a ton of gear up Chilkoot Pass for a chance at gold?
sources: Pierre Berton - Klondike: The Last Great Gold Rush, 1896-1899 (1958)
T.A. Rickard - Through the Yukon and Alaska (1909)

National Park Service - Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park Archives

beats.text: It is July eighteen ninety-seven. You are twenty-two years old, standing on the crowded docks of Seattle.
A steamship named the Portland just tied up, carrying sixty-eight miners and more than a ton of pure gold.
That young fool staring at the heavy leather sacks was me. My name is Walt Becker. Tonight, I will tell you how we chased a dream into the frozen North.
The city went mad overnight. Clerks quit their jobs, doctors left their clinics, and shopkeepers sold everything to buy a ticket North.
I had three hundred dollars saved from farm work. I bought passage on a rusted steamer bound for Dyea, Alaska.
The papers called it the last great adventure of the century. They promised gold lying in creek beds like yellow gravel.
beats.label: SEATTLE TO DYEA

beats.text: On the crowded deck, I met Sam Miller, a blacksmith from Ohio. We agreed to pool our money and travel as partners.
Sam was strong as an ox and always had a warm smile. We thought we would be rich before Christmas.
When our ship pulled into the muddy inlet of Dyea, Alaska, reality hit us like a bucket of ice water.
There was no town, no docks, and no hotel. Just thousands of desperate men thrown onto a stony beach in the freezing rain.
We pitched a crude tent in the mud, shivering as cold ocean wind whipped off the inlet waves.
We had no idea that the real test had not even begun.
By autumn, winter was already creeping down from the mountain peaks, coating the valley in gray slush.
At the border, the Canadian North-West Mounted Police posted a strict legal warning for every stampeder.
beats.label: ONE TON

beats.text: Inspector Charles Constantine made the law clear. No man could enter Canada without two thousand pounds of food and survival gear.
Two thousand pounds. One whole ton of supplies per person, meant to keep a miner alive for one full year in the North.
The mandatory list required five hundred pounds of flour, one hundred pounds of bacon, dried beans, coffee, blankets, and hand tools.
beats.label: 500 LBS FLOUR

beats.text: Sam and I spent nearly all our remaining cash buying sacks of flour and salted pork at outrageous frontier prices.
We had no pack horses. Every single pound had to be carried on our own backs, forty or fifty pounds at a time.
The trail from Dyea to the base of the pass was twenty-six miles of thick mud, tree roots, and icy streams.
We hauled fifty pounds five miles up, dropped the load on the snow, and walked five miles back for the next bundle.
To move two tons of gear, Sam and I had to walk that muddy mountain trail back and forth forty times.
Before we even saw a mountain peak, we had walked over one thousand miles carrying heavy packs.
At night, we slept under wet canvas tents, shivering as the freezing rain turned into thick winter snow.
Sam developed a deep, rattling cough that never quite went away, but he refused to stop hauling.
By November, the trail disappeared under five feet of fresh snow. We reached the foot of Chilkoot Pass.
Looking up at that sheer wall of white ice, my heart dropped straight into my leather boots.
And the worst part of the mountain was still waiting for us.
Chilkoot Pass rose thirty-five hundred feet into freezing clouds, a steep wall of solid snow and ice.
Miners had carved fifteen hundred steps straight up the face of the snow slope. We called them the Golden Stairs.
The slope was forty-five degrees steep. You had to kick your heavy leather boots into the step ahead of you.
Thousands of men climbed in single file, locked shoulder to shoulder like an endless black snake on the white ice.
If you stepped out of line to rest, you might wait two hours before anyone would let you back into line.
Each trip up the Golden Stairs took six agonizing hours under a heavy fifty-pound pack.
Let me ask you something. If you had to climb an icy mountain forty times with heavy bags, would you turn back or press on? Tell me in the comments.
Indigenous Tlingit packers helped carry loads for those who could pay, charging up to fifty cents a pound.
Fifty cents a pound was a fortune in eighteen ninety-seven, but many men had no strength left to haul.
beats.label: 50 CENTS / LB

beats.text: The weather on the pass was merciless. Sudden blizzards dropped temperatures to forty below zero within minutes.
One morning, an avalanche swept down the mountain, burying sixty men under deep snow.
Sam and I dug with our bare hands for three hours, pulling two men out alive before frost bit our fingers.
By mid-December, after three brutal months of constant climbing, our entire ton of gear was finally atop the pass.
We stood at the Canadian border post, exhausted, battered, but victorious.
The Mountie inspector checked off our supplies, stamped our papers, and welcomed us into the Yukon territory.
We sledded our two thousand pounds of gear down to Lake Bennett and set up winter camp.
Now we had to wait six long winter months for the ice on the river to thaw.
Winter at Lake Bennett was quiet, cold, and deadly.
Thirty thousand people were camped around Lake Bennett, waiting for spring to melt the thick lake ice.
A massive tent city had sprung up on the frozen shore. It was the largest town of canvas in the world.
To travel five hundred miles down the Yukon River to the goldfields, every team needed a wooden boat.
There were no sawmills. We had to chop down massive pine trees and haul the heavy logs on sleds.
We dug a saw pit six feet into the frozen earth. Sam stood down in the pit while I stood above.
For weeks, sawdust poured down into Sam's face as we pulled a six-foot hand saw up and down.
We cut hundreds of feet of green pine lumber, our hands blistered and bleeding from the raw work.
We sealed the wooden seams with hot pitch and frayed rope to make our scow boat watertight.
beats.label: PITCH & OAKUM

beats.text: We named our boat the Northern Star. She was ugly and heavy, but she was strong.
Sam painted our boat's name on the bow in dark red paint. For a moment, we felt like true pioneers.
On May twenty-ninth, eighteen ninety-eight, the ice on Lake Bennett suddenly cracked with a roar like cannon fire.
Within hours, seven thousand handmade boats pushed off into the cold water at the exact same time.
It was an astonishing armada of wooden rafts, skiffs, and canoes drifting down the clear blue lakes.
The water carried us northward toward the Klondike River. Gold was only two hundred miles away.
We thought the worst of our hardships were behind us as the current pulled our boat along.
Then we heard the roaring thunder of Miles Canyon.
The Yukon River was about to claim its price.
Miles Canyon was a narrow basalt gorge where the roaring river squeezed into a raging white torrent.
Swirling whirlpools and jagged black rocks swallowed wooden boats whole. Dozens of men had already drowned.
Inspector Jack Norwood of the Mounties halted all unguided boats at the canyon entrance for safety.
Experienced boat pilots charged twenty-five dollars to steer rafts through the deadly Whitehorse Rapids.
beats.label: PILOT $25

beats.text: Sam and I did not have twenty-five dollars left. We had to pilot our own heavy wooden scow.
Sam took the bow sweep and I grabbed the stern oar. We plunged into the roaring white foam.
The wall of water threw our heavy boat like a pine toothpick. Water surged over the wooden sides!
Sam yelled at the top of his lungs, pulling his oar with every ounce of strength he had left.
We shot through the roaring canyon in three terrifying minutes and spun out into calm water below.
We were soaked to the skin and half our flour sacks were ruined, but we were alive.
We bailed out the boat, dried our gear in the spring sun, and drifted the final miles.
On June eighth, eighteen ninety-eight, our boat rounded the river bend and Dawson City appeared.
What we found in Dawson was not what any of us had dreamed.
Dawson City was a booming town built on a muddy swamp, packed with forty thousand desperate souls.
Log cabins, dance halls, and muddy streets were jammed with stampeders who had arrived too late.
Every single gold claim on Bonanza Creek had been staked two years earlier, in eighteen ninety-six.
Prices in town were insane. Fresh eggs cost three dollars each, and a single loaf of bread was one dollar.
beats.label: EGGS $3 EACH

beats.text: Men who had carried a ton of supplies across mountains were selling their gear just to buy a steamboat ticket home.
Scurvy broke out in the overcrowded camps. Sam's gums bled and his legs grew swollen and dark.
I spent our last silver coins on a jar of spruce-needle tea and raw potatoes to save Sam's life.
Out of one hundred thousand men who set out for the Klondike, only four thousand ever found gold.
Sam and I never found gold. In August, we worked as deckhands on a riverboat to pay for our passage south.
If you have stayed with me this far, leave a like and subscribe; that is how I know you want more stories like this one.
We returned home to Ohio without a single ounce of gold, but with something far more precious.
We survived the greatest winter trek in human history, shoulder to shoulder with men who never quit.
That gold rush made boys into men, and made brothers out of strangers.
The gold in the ground stays frozen, but the warmth of those old memories keeps me going by this stove. Goodnight, my friends.
